title: Review: Cell theory, microscopes and magnification; Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure; Protein secretion and the endomembrane system; Prokaryotic cells and viruses
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CE04a#t2 term and clue written for the game; CE04a#t3 term and clue written for the game; CE04b#t3 term and clue written for the game; CE03#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CE01a#N.12, CE02a#N.11a, CE03#N.8b, CE04a#N.13a, CE04b#N.2a, CE01a#N.6, CE02a#N.8a, CE04a#N.3a, CE04b#N.5, CE01a#N.9, CE02a#N.12. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nucleoid
items.clue: Region of cytoplasm where a bacterium's circular DNA lies free

items.label: Peptidoglycan
items.clue: The material of the wall outside a bacterium's plasma membrane

items.label: Reverse transcriptase
items.clue: Enzyme carried by HIV; having it is what makes HIV a retrovirus

items.label: Glycoproteins
items.clue: Molecules made when carbohydrate chains are added to polypeptides

questions.stem: A micrograph shows a pollen grain 60 mm across. A scale bar on the micrograph is 20 mm long and is labelled 10 µm. What is the actual diameter of the pollen grain?

options.text: 3 µm
30 µm
60 µm
120 µm

questions.explanation: Magnification = 20 000 µm ÷ 10 µm = ×2000. Actual size = 60 000 µm ÷ 2000 = 30 µm.

questions.stem: In an electron micrograph of an animal cell, a structure appears as a discrete stack of curved, flattened membrane sacs with small vesicles budding from its edges and no ribosomes attached. Which structure is it?

options.text: Golgi apparatus, where proteins are modified and packaged
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, where lipids are made
Mitochondrion, where aerobic cell respiration is carried out
Rough endoplasmic reticulum, where secreted proteins are made

questions.explanation: A stack of curved sacs, separate from the nuclear envelope, with no ribosomes and vesicles budding from its edges as proteins are packaged for transport.

questions.stem: A vesicle from the Golgi apparatus carries a protein to the plasma membrane for secretion. What happens to the membrane of the vesicle when the protein is released?

options.text: It fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it.
It passes out through the plasma membrane and is lost from the cell.
It is broken down into phospholipids reused to build the next vesicle.
It stays joined to the Golgi apparatus as a channel for more protein.

questions.explanation: In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. Its phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph shows a cell about 3 µm long. It has a cell wall, a paler fibrous region of DNA not enclosed by any membrane, many small dense granules, and no membrane-bound organelles. How should the cell be classified?

options.text: As a plant cell, because a cell wall is found only around the cells of plants.
As a eukaryote, because the region containing DNA must be a nucleus, as every cell has one.
As a prokaryote, because its DNA lies in a nucleoid region and it has no membrane-bound organelles.
As a eukaryote, because prokaryotic cells are too simple to contain any ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell

questions.explanation: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.stem: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?

options.text: 7.5 µm

questions.explanation: Actual size = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm): the typical diameter of a red blood cell.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a membrane-bound organelle of a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes that synthesise proteins.
Mitochondria are bounded by a single membrane folded inward to form cristae.
Lysosomes are vesicles bounded by a single membrane that contain hydrolytic enzymes.
Secretory vesicles are lysosomes under another name, digesting worn-out organelles.

questions.explanation: Lysosomes are single-membrane sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes, kept separate from the rest of the cytoplasm, that digest material taken in and worn-out organelles.

questions.stem: Which description of the structure of a Bacillus cell is correct?

options.text: A loop of naked DNA lies in the cytoplasm, and proteins are made on 70S ribosomes.
The DNA is enclosed by a nuclear membrane inside a small nucleus within the cytoplasm.
The cell wall outside the plasma membrane is built from long parallel fibres of cellulose.
The DNA loop is wound around histone proteins to package it within the nucleoid region.

questions.explanation: A Gram-positive eubacterium such as Bacillus has a cell wall, a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a loop lying in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes on which its proteins are synthesised.

questions.stem: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?

options.text: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolises them to build copies of itself.
It must first acquire a DNA molecule, because one RNA strand cannot act as genetic material.

questions.stem: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?

options.text: 1.1 mm

questions.explanation: 100 µm ÷ 40 = 2.5 µm per division with this objective. 44 × 2.5 µm = 110 µm = 0.11 mm.

questions.stem: An electron micrograph of a cell shows a large amount of rough ER, a large Golgi and many small vesicles close to the cell surface. What does this cell most likely do?

options.text: It makes large amounts of lipid, using the ribosomes on its ER.
It digests engulfed bacteria, using the enzymes in its many vesicles.
It makes proteins, such as enzymes, and releases them from the cell.
It makes proteins in the Golgi, which the ER then packs into vesicles.

questions.explanation: RER makes proteins; the Golgi modifies and packages them; vesicles carry them to the surface for release.
